Reuters reports that Apple has won a lawsuit filed against it for allegedly failing to prevent child sexual abuse material from being stored and shared via iCloud. Here's what you need to know.

Apple is protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act

According to Reuters, U.S. District Court Judge Noël Wise has dismissed a proposed class action filed in 2024, with prejudice. The lawsuit accused Apple of "failing to prevent the spread of child sexual abuse material through its iCloud data storage platform."

In the complaint, two survivors, identified under the pseudonyms Amy and Jessica, alleged that images of their childhood abuse continued to circulate via iCloud, and that Apple knowingly refused to use available tools to detect and report known child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

The lawsuit specifically pointed to Apple's decision to abandon NeuralHash—a system Apple announced in 2021 that would have compared images uploaded to iCloud against a database of identified abuse material.

Amy and Jessica sought to file a class action on behalf of thousands of other survivors. Citing subsequent court documents, Reuters reported that the proposed class was estimated to include 2,680 individuals, with "recoverable damages estimated at up to $32.8 billion."

They argued that all members of the proposed class were affected by the same Apple policies and product decisions, and that handling their claims together would reduce the burden and trauma of filing separate lawsuits. The complaint stated:

Returning to the court's dismissal, Reuters noted that Judge Wise stated that "the lawsuit seeks to hold Apple liable for failing to remove or block user-generated content, bringing such claims within the scope of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a federal law enacted in 1996."

In short, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act generally shields online service providers from legal liability as publishers of content created by their users. This provision has long been at the center of debates over how much responsibility tech companies should bear for material shared on their platforms.

Reuters noted that although the case was dismissed with prejudice—meaning it cannot be refiled—"the plaintiffs' lead attorney, James Marsh, said they are considering an appeal and evaluating whether other legal claims are available."
